title: Pythagoras' Theorem
description: Using a² + b² = c² to find unknown sides in right-angled triangles, Pythagorean triples, and 2D and 3D applications.

notes.heading: The Theorem and Finding the Hypotenuse
notes.body: In any right-angled triangle: a² + b² = c², where c is the hypotenuse (side opposite the right angle, always longest). To find the hypotenuse: c = √(a²+b²). Example: legs 3 and 4 → c = √(9+16) = 5.

notes.heading: Finding a Shorter Side and Pythagorean Triples
notes.body: To find a shorter side: a = √(c²−b²). Example: hypotenuse 13, leg 5 → a = √(169−25) = 12. Pythagorean triples: integer sets satisfying the theorem — 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25. Multiples also work (6-8-10 = 2× 3-4-5).

notes.heading: Testing for Right Angles and Distance in 2D
notes.body: To test if triangle is right-angled: check if a²+b²=c² (where c is the longest). If yes → right-angled; if a²+b²>c² → acute; if a²+b²<c² → obtuse. Distance between (x₁,y₁) and (x₂,y₂): d = √((x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)²) — a direct Pythagoras application.

notes.heading: 3D Applications
notes.body: Space diagonal of cuboid (l×w×h): first find base diagonal d₁=√(l²+w²), then space diagonal d=√(d₁²+h²) = √(l²+w²+h²). Example: 3×4×12: base=5, space=√(25+144)=13.

notes.heading: 📌 Converse of Pythagoras' Theorem
notes.body: The converse lets you test whether a triangle is right-angled: if the longest side squared equals the sum of the other two sides squared, then the triangle contains a $90^\circ$ angle. For sides $a$, $b$, $c$ with $c$ longest: if $a^2+b^2=c^2$, the triangle is right-angled; if $a^2+b^2>c^2$, it is acute; if $a^2+b^2<c^2$, it is obtuse.

notes.heading: 💡 Worked Example: Ladder against a Wall
notes.body: A ladder leans against a vertical wall with its foot 1.5 m from the wall and reaches 4 m up the wall. The ladder length $l$ is the hypotenuse: $$l = \sqrt{1.5^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{2.25 + 16} = \sqrt{18.25} \approx 4.27 \text{ m}.$$

notes.heading: ⚠️ Common Mistake: Adding Before Squaring
notes.body: A common error is to add the two legs first and then square: $(a+b)^2$ instead of $a^2+b^2$. This is wrong because the theorem requires each leg to be squared before adding. Check: for legs 3 and 4, $(3+4)^2=49$, but $3^2+4^2=25$ and $\sqrt{25}=5$ is the correct hypotenuse.
